chapters.title: Everything He Bought, Built and Buried

blocks.text: Bernard Arnault is usually described as a man with one company. That hides most of the story. Before LVMH there was a family builder and a Florida housing project that went wrong. After LVMH came an online bank, an auction house, a supermarket bet and a fashion house that never made a profit. This chapter walks through all of them in order.

One warning about the list. LVMH owns more than 75 houses, and many of them, like Moët & Chandon and Hennessy, came with the group when he took control. So we count only the businesses he chose: the ones he bought, started, fought for or walked away from. __Watch the pattern as you read: almost nothing here starts with his own cash alone. He keeps finding other people's money, and he keeps selling what he does not want.__
Count the failures too. There are more than you think.
Before luxury: bricks and condos

blocks.name: Ferret-Savinel, then Ferinel
blocks.idea: A family building firm from Roubaix in northern France, founded by his grandfather in 1922. The new idea was to stop doing construction work and instead sell holiday homes by the sea. Its advertising promised buyers they could become owners at the seaside.
blocks.decision: Arnault was a young engineer, fresh from École Polytechnique, and he pushed his father to drop construction for property development. He also moved early into timeshares on the Riviera, where buyers pay for a set share of a holiday home.
blocks.howStarted: He joined the family firm in 1971, straight after graduating. Les Echos says he was running it by 1976, at age 27, when it was reshaped and renamed. When he left for America in 1981 he handed the keys to Michel Lefebvre, his trusted right-hand man.
blocks.funding: Family money. Selling the construction arm reportedly raised 40 million francs, which went into the new property business.
blocks.whatHappened: Ferinel became Arnault's training ground and stayed in the group long after he moved to fashion. It was later renamed Groupe George V. By October 1995 Les Echos was reporting that it was about to be sold to Compagnie Générale des Eaux, which would end his original line of work.
blocks.lesson: Your first business does not have to be the big idea. It can simply be the place you learn to do deals.

blocks.name: Ferinel Inc., Florida
blocks.idea: Build apartments and houses in Florida during a construction boom. The dollar then cost only 5 francs, which gave a Frenchman with francs a lot of buying power.
blocks.decision: François Mitterrand won the French presidency in May 1981, and Arnault judged it a bad moment to invest at home. He looked abroad and stuck to what he knew: property.
blocks.howStarted: In May 1982 he flew to New York and settled with his wife and two children in New Rochelle. He rented an office on the 45th floor of the Rockefeller Center. The actual building happened in Florida.
blocks.funding: Partner investors, through a US subsidiary of Ferinel. The first project alone was a $30 million programme. We found no public breakdown of how much was Arnault's own money.
blocks.whatHappened: The first project was a 19-storey tower on Hutchinson Island. He claimed a $3 million profit on it, which a former partner disputed. A second set of houses at West Palm Beach made a 5% margin by his own account. The third, the Banyon Club near Palm Beach airport, went wrong when the insurance company guaranteeing his investors collapsed, and he handed it to a colleague. Les Echos later wrote that American property kings had made him eat dust.
blocks.lesson: A failed venture can still pay you back in contacts. In America he met a Lazard banker and an executive tied to Boussac's state shareholder. Both mattered within two years.

blocks.text: The Florida flop gave him the two contacts that led to Dior.

There is a small, strange souvenir from those years. When Arnault left, he sold his Mediterranean-style house near New York to a neighbour, the media mogul John Kluge. Kluge simply had it removed because it blocked his view. Arnault told Forbes the lesson he took: when something must be done, Americans just do it, while the French have good ideas and rarely act on them.
The wreck that held a jewel

blocks.name: Boussac Saint-Frères
blocks.idea: A collapsed textile group with mills, a nappy brand, a furniture chain and department stores. France's government wanted someone to save the jobs. Arnault wanted one thing inside it: Christian Dior.
blocks.decision: He saw Dior as the start of a luxury empire for a rising global middle class. He beat rival bidders by offering the plan the government judged the least painful in jobs. Les Echos later called the group a dead dog hiding nuggets of gold: Dior, Au Bon Marché and Conforama.
blocks.howStarted: A friend, Michel Godé, showed him the file when he came home in 1984. On 16 December 1984 he wrote to Prime Minister Laurent Fabius asking for state support, and the next day the government said yes.
blocks.funding: A 400 million franc round assembled with Lazard's Antoine Bernheim. Arnault's side put in only 90 million francs, and part of that was reportedly a loan from state-owned bank Crédit Lyonnais. The rest came from Lazard, Banque Worms, units of Elf and Total, and a Lebanese fund called Finial Holding. English-language sources give $15 million of family money in an $80 million deal.
blocks.whatHappened: He turned it profitable within about two years, by cutting thousands of jobs and selling most of the group. By 1988 the textile empire had gone. The EU later ordered 338.56 million francs of the state aid to be repaid. The full story, including the broken promises, is in the next chapter.
blocks.lesson: Look inside failing companies for the one asset that is worth more than the whole thing. Then be honest about the human cost of getting it.

blocks.name: Peaudouce, the textile mills and Conforama
blocks.idea: Three businesses he inherited from Boussac and did not want: France's biggest nappy maker, the cotton mills, and a profitable furniture chain with 140 stores.
blocks.decision: Luxury investors disliked seeing furniture mixed with fashion. Selling gave him cash and a cleaner story.
blocks.howStarted: He did not start these. He found buyers one by one: Sweden for nappies, the Prouvost wool group for textiles, and François Pinault for furniture.
blocks.funding: No new money was needed. These sales were the money. They funded his next move.
blocks.whatHappened: Peaudouce went to Swedish group Mölnlycke, part of SCA, in 1988. On 20 May 1988 the textile arm, down to 3,000 staff, went to Prouvost in exchange for shares. In 1991 Pinault paid between 3.1 and 3.2 billion francs in cash plus further share deals for control of Conforama. Arnault had reportedly asked for 6 billion a year earlier.
blocks.lesson: Sell what does not fit, even if it is profitable. But notice who bought Conforama. Eight years later that same buyer took Gucci from him.

blocks.name: Christian Dior
blocks.idea: A famous couture name spread thin across hundreds of licensing deals, whose perfume arm had been sold off years earlier. Arnault's bet was that the name itself was the most valuable thing in French business.
blocks.decision: He liked to tell a story about asking a New York taxi driver what he knew about France. The driver could not name the president, but he knew Christian Dior.
blocks.howStarted: It came inside Boussac. He kept it when everything else was sold. He then cut the licences hard, from 280 in 1989 to about 120 by the mid-1990s, and opened Dior's own shops in Asia.
blocks.funding: The Boussac round. In 1991 he also sold a minority slice on the stock market in an IPO. An IPO is when a private company first sells shares to the public.
blocks.whatHappened: Couture sales rose from 673 million francs in 1990 to just over 1 billion in 1995. He hired John Galliano to shock a sleepy house awake. The Dior holding company became the tool he used to control LVMH. In 2017 LVMH bought Christian Dior Couture for €6.5 billion, finally reuniting fashion and perfume under one roof.
blocks.lesson: A brand can be cheapened by too many licences. Fewer logos, more control, higher value.

blocks.name: Christian Lacroix
blocks.idea: A new couture house. Start at the very top with haute couture, then earn real money from ready-to-wear, accessories and perfume. It was the same system that had made older houses rich.
blocks.decision: Arnault spotted a star designer and asked him to build a house from nothing. It remains the only brand he ever started from scratch, rather than buying.
blocks.howStarted: The house opened in 1987, based in an 18th-century Paris palace. The first collection was an instant sensation, compared in the press to the buzz around Dior's New Look.
blocks.funding: His own group's money. The Independent wrote that he launched it with his own money. The exact amount has never been published as far as we could find.
blocks.whatHappened: It never made a profit, in all its years. LVMH sold it in January 2005 to the Falic brothers, Florida duty-free retailers, for a reported €2 million. Annual sales then were about €35 million. In May 2009 it filed for court protection, and that December the couture and ready-to-wear lines were dropped and staff fell from 124 to about 12.
blocks.lesson: Applause is not revenue. Even the best deal-maker in luxury could not make a brand work just because the critics loved it.

blocks.text: His only from-scratch brand never made a cent of profit.

blocks.name: Celine
blocks.idea: A Paris leather-goods label, then best known for its loafers. It added a second name to his growing plan for a luxury supermarket.
blocks.decision: Dior alone could not make a group. He wanted several names under one roof.
blocks.howStarted: He bought into it in 1987, while the LVMH fight was still ahead of him.
blocks.funding: The 1987 price is not in the sources we read. In 1991 Financière Agache sold all of it to Le Bon Marché, another Arnault company, for 1.075 billion francs.
blocks.whatHappened: In 1996 Celine moved inside LVMH for 2.7 billion francs, about $540 million. In 2025 its new designer, Michael Rider, was part of LVMH's creative reshuffle.
blocks.lesson: Moving a business between your own companies raises fair questions from outside shareholders. Investors watch the price you set.

blocks.text: The prize

blocks.name: LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton
blocks.idea: The merger of Louis Vuitton luggage with Moët Hennessy champagne and cognac, formed in June 1987. Arnault did not create it. He saw that two feuding bosses had made it vulnerable, and he walked through the gap.
blocks.decision: Vuitton's Henry Racamier invited him in as an ally against Moët's Alain Chevalier. Arnault instead sided with neither and took the whole thing. The group also owned the Dior perfume business, the one part of the Dior name he lacked.
blocks.howStarted: He entered in mid-1988 with Guinness as a partner, through a company called Jacques Rober, owned 60% by Dior and 40% by Guinness.
blocks.funding: About 7.3 billion francs, raised through a giant Dior share sale to institutions, plus Guinness. Five layers of holding companies sat between his family and LVMH.
blocks.whatHappened: He became chairman in January 1989 and won the final court ruling in April 1990. In 2025 the group made €80.8 billion in revenue and €17.8 billion in operating profit. Its stock market value passed $500 billion in 2023, and it became the first European company to reach that mark.
blocks.lesson: When the people in charge are fighting each other, the company is for sale, whether they know it or not.

blocks.name: The Guinness alliance
blocks.idea: A swap of shareholdings with Britain's Guinness, which already sold Moët and Hennessy around the world. Each company held 24% of the other.
blocks.decision: He needed a heavyweight friend to win LVMH. Guinness needed to protect its lucrative drinks distribution.
blocks.howStarted: Guinness came in through Alain Chevalier, who had asked its boss for help against a takeover. Arnault then won Guinness over to his own side.
blocks.funding: Cross-shareholdings, not cash from outside investors. In January 1994 the deal was unwound. Guinness took 34% of Moët Hennessy, and LVMH received 11 billion francs.
blocks.whatHappened: LVMH's share price fell 3.42% on the 1994 news, while Guinness jumped 10.8%. Then in 1997 Arnault tried to block Guinness's merger with GrandMet and walked away with about £500 million in cash and special dividends. Chapter four tells that story.
blocks.lesson: Partners are useful, until they are not. Write down early exactly what happens if one of you changes.

blocks.name: Guerlain, Kenzo, Berluti, Loewe and the 1990s shopping list
blocks.idea: Old family names in perfume, fashion, shoes and leather, bought one at a time.
blocks.decision: The Guinness cash arrived in 1994, about $1.9 billion, and he told BusinessWeek he would spend it on luxury companies. Guerlain's family did not want to sell, so he offered them a partnership instead.
blocks.howStarted: Each deal was a negotiation with one family. LVMH already held about 14–15% of Guerlain before the 1994 deal.
blocks.funding: Often shares, not cash. The Guerlain family got 4.35 million Christian Dior shares, worth 1.96 billion francs, for 51.2% of their holding company. Kenzo was bought for $80 million in 1993. Loewe followed in 1996.
blocks.whatHappened: The Guerlains kept narrow voting control at first, and also ended up owning 12% of Dior. Guerlain was still gaining sales in 2026. These smaller deals mostly lasted, which is more than can be said for the bigger trophies of the late 1990s.
blocks.lesson: If a family will not sell for cash, offer them shares in your future. It lets them feel like partners, not losers.

blocks.name: DFS (Duty Free Shoppers)
blocks.idea: The world's biggest chain of duty-free shops. Owning it meant owning the place where wealthy travellers, especially from Japan, bought luxury goods.
blocks.decision: He wanted to control where luxury goods were sold, not only make them. Investors pushed LVMH shares up 14% in a week at first.
blocks.howStarted: Co-founder Chuck Feeney and fellow shareholder Alan Parker agreed to sell. The other co-founder, Robert Miller, tried in court to block it, failed, and stayed on as an unhappy minority partner with about 38%.
blocks.funding: $2.47 billion for 58.75%, closed in January 1997. LVMH sold about a third of its Guinness shares, for about $1 billion, to help pay.
blocks.whatHappened: Months later the Asian financial crisis hit, and Miller said the business fell fast. It recovered on Chinese travellers, then never got back to its 2019 level after the pandemic. In 2026 LVMH sold the Hong Kong and Macau shops to China Tourism Group for an estimated $294 million, and by October it said most of DFS had been sold.
blocks.lesson: Buying a customer base means buying its risk. DFS was built on Japanese travellers, and later on Chinese ones.

blocks.name: Sephora
blocks.idea: A French perfume chain with a new idea: let shoppers walk in and try everything themselves, instead of asking a sales assistant behind a counter.
blocks.decision: With DFS already bought, LVMH called itself the world's leading seller of perfume and beauty. Founder Dominique Mandonnaud wanted out at 50 and was thinking about an IPO. Suez's boss said LVMH won because it could take the chain worldwide.
blocks.howStarted: LVMH bought out everyone at once: the founder and three financial backers. The chain then had 54 stores and $225 million in sales.
blocks.funding: LVMH's own money: 1.6 billion francs, about $262 million, which was more than 30 times its expected profit.
blocks.whatHappened: Expansion was brutal, from 57 stores to 462 in three years. In 2001 it pulled out of Japan, and analysts estimated a global operating loss near $154 million, with sale rumours everywhere. LVMH denied it was selling. By 2025 Sephora was the global leader, and the selective retail division made €1.78 billion in operating profit.
blocks.lesson: The deal everyone calls genius today looked like the worst one on the list in 2001. Be careful judging a bet after only four years.

blocks.text: Almost sold in 2001. Now one of his best businesses. Read twice.

blocks.name: Marc Jacobs
blocks.idea: A young New York designer's label, bought together with the designer's talent. Jacobs would also design womenswear for Louis Vuitton.
blocks.decision: He wanted American designers to help win America, which he had made a priority.
blocks.howStarted: LVMH took a majority stake in 1997. Jacobs stayed at Louis Vuitton until 2013.
blocks.funding: LVMH's money. The price of the 1997 stake was not published in the sources we read.
blocks.whatHappened: His own label became a long search for a buyer. In May 2026 LVMH agreed to sell it to WHP Global and G-III, who raised up to $850 million. The sale closed on 1 September 2026, with Jacobs staying as creative director.
blocks.lesson: Sometimes the real prize in a deal is the person. This one gave Louis Vuitton the same designer for 16 years.

blocks.name: Château d'Yquem and Château Cheval Blanc
blocks.idea: Two of the most famous wine estates on earth, both family-owned for generations. Very little wine, very high prices.
blocks.decision: Yquem had about 50 shareholders, and many wanted to cash out. Arnault bought from them over the head of the man who ran it, Count Alexandre de Lur Saluces. Cheval Blanc was a personal purchase, not through LVMH, with his Belgian tennis partner Albert Frère.
blocks.howStarted: The Yquem buying began in late 1996. Lur Saluces sued repeatedly. Cheval Blanc was sold by a family of 42 owners in autumn 1998. Liliane Bettencourt of L'Oréal had also shown interest.
blocks.funding: LVMH paid a reported $101 million for its first Yquem stake. Arnault and Frère split Cheval Blanc equally at a reported 860 million francs, a record price per hectare at the time.
blocks.whatHappened: In April 1999 the fight ended over dinner, when Lur Saluces served Arnault an 1899 Yquem and agreed to sell. LVMH ended up with about 64%. Cheval Blanc still names Arnault and Frère as the buyers in its own history.
blocks.lesson: Patience beats a loud enemy. He spent over two years in court, then offered the count a way to stay with dignity.

blocks.text: The late-1990s spree, and the bills

blocks.name: Gucci
blocks.idea: Buy the hottest brand in fashion before anyone else could. Gucci was an Italian name then flying under Domenico De Sole and Tom Ford.
blocks.decision: He started buying quietly, called it passive, and then refused to sign a standstill deal limiting his stake.
blocks.howStarted: The stake became public on 6 January 1999 at 5%. By 26 January it was 34.4%. He even bought a 9.5% block from Prada's Patrizio Bertelli.
blocks.funding: LVMH itself. How it funded the stake is not spelled out in the sources we read. It later offered $81 and then $85 a share for the whole company.
blocks.whatHappened: Gucci diluted him from 34.4% to about 20% and sold 42% to François Pinault's PPR for $3 billion. A Dutch court upheld it. After two and a half years of lawsuits LVMH sold out in 2001 and booked a €774 million gain. He lost the brand and won the money. Full story in chapter four.
blocks.lesson: You can lose the war and still profit, if you bought well and stay a problem until someone pays you to leave.

blocks.name: Fendi
blocks.idea: A Rome family fashion house with five sisters, furs, Karl Lagerfeld, and the hit Baguette bag.
blocks.decision: Partly to win, partly to deny. An analyst at the time said LVMH paid a high price both for growth and to stop Gucci buying it.
blocks.howStarted: LVMH teamed up with Prada, bidding jointly against Gucci in October 1999. The deal was signed late at night in Rome with champagne.
blocks.funding: An estimated $545 million between LVMH and Prada for 51%. That was more than 33 times Fendi's profit, in an industry where 25 was considered very high.
blocks.whatHappened: Sales flattened at first. In November 2001 Prada, deep in debt, sold LVMH its half for about €295 million. LVMH reached 84% in 2003.
blocks.lesson: A rival's bad year is your best buying chance. Prada's debt problem handed LVMH control.

blocks.name: TAG Heuer, Zenith, Chaumet and the watch push
blocks.idea: Build a third leg in watches and jewellery, where Cartier's owner was already strong.
blocks.decision: He was buying everything in luxury at the time, and rivals were copying his model.
blocks.howStarted: All three deals landed in 1999, the same year as the Gucci fight. Hublot followed in 2008.
blocks.funding: LVMH itself. The $739 million bid for 50.1% of TAG Heuer is the only price in the sources we read.
blocks.whatHappened: The start was weak. In 2001 LVMH's watch and jewellery margins were about 7%, below rivals at 10%. The later Bulgari and Tiffany deals built the division, which earned €1.5 billion in 2025.
blocks.lesson: Buying a business does not buy expertise in that business. That can take a decade.

blocks.name: Phillips auction house
blocks.idea: Take the old number-three auctioneer and turn it into a real rival to Sotheby's and Christie's.
blocks.decision: The family collects art, and he vowed to make Phillips a high-end rival to the two giants. He had at one point thought of buying Sotheby's.
blocks.howStarted: He bought Phillips in November 1999, then merged it with the Geneva dealers Simon de Pury and Daniella Luxembourg.
blocks.funding: LVMH paid $97 million or $115 million, depending on the report. The Wall Street Journal estimated another $250 million was then poured in.
blocks.whatHappened: The house paid huge sums to win collections and hire specialists away. It never turned a profit under him. In February 2002 he handed control to de Pury and Luxembourg, cutting LVMH's stake to 27.5%. The New York Times called it one of several regrettable ventures.
blocks.lesson: Passion is a poor reason to enter a two-player market. Those two have better clients, and you pay extra for every client you steal.

blocks.name: Europ@web
blocks.idea: Europe's biggest internet investment fund. It would back start-ups in Europe and help American web companies build brands, an area he said he understood better than they did.
blocks.decision: The whole world had internet fever. He argued that brands would matter online, which was his speciality. Unusually, this was personal money, not LVMH's.
blocks.howStarted: He launched it on 30 June 1999 from Groupe Arnault, already holding stakes in eBay, Cisco, Webvan and others. It grew to more than 50 holdings and nine offices.
blocks.funding: €500 million from his own fortune, about $516 million then.
blocks.whatHappened: In late 2000 his bankers estimated his tech holdings at $2.5–3.5 billion. By then the planned IPO had already been pulled, in June 2000. He persuaded Suez to pay €300 million for 30% of part of the portfolio just in time. By September 2001 seven of the nine offices had shut, and one €30 million stake in QXL was worth under €3 million.
blocks.lesson: When you are late to a boom, the smart move is to sell part of your bet to someone later than you.

blocks.name: Boo.com
blocks.idea: A stylish website selling designer clothes, and one of the most talked-about start-ups in Europe.
blocks.decision: It fitted his theory that the internet would need brands.
blocks.howStarted: It launched in 1999 with a huge marketing budget, and he was among the lead backers along with Italy's Benetton family.
blocks.funding: His private investment, alongside other investors. His exact amount has not been published.
blocks.whatHappened: It burned an estimated $130 million and made just over $1 million in sales. When it asked for more money in May 2000, Arnault and the Benettons said no, and a British court appointed liquidators. It was Europe's first big internet collapse.
blocks.lesson: A famous backer is not a business model. Check sales first, and the website's beauty last.

blocks.name: Zebank
blocks.idea: An online bank. The early plan went by the name Ze Project.
blocks.decision: Internet banks were launching everywhere. Europ@web studied an online broker first, and then chose banking.
blocks.howStarted: The bank Dexia joined in. Commercial operations began in early 2001.
blocks.funding: A budget of €110 million from Europ@web and Dexia.
blocks.whatHappened: It claimed 80,000 accounts by autumn 2001 but had burned through its cash. In 2002 Arnault sold it to Britain's Egg for €5.5 million, about 5 cents for every euro budgeted. Egg itself pulled out of France in 2005 after heavy losses.
blocks.lesson: Winning customers is not the same as having a business. Check how long your cash lasts.

blocks.name: LibertySurf
blocks.idea: A free French internet service provider, which grew to 700,000 active customers.
blocks.decision: It was his team's own creation, hatched inside Groupe Arnault in March 1999, and the proof that his incubator idea could work.
blocks.howStarted: An in-house team built it and floated it on the stock market in March 2000, right at the top of the boom.
blocks.funding: About €55 million from Arnault's side.
blocks.whatHappened: At one point it showed nearly €1 billion in paper gains. When the bubble burst he sold to Tiscali for €237 million, of which €71 million was cash. That was a rare win for the fund.
blocks.lesson: Paper gains are not gains. He took about a quarter of the peak and still made four times his money.

blocks.name: eLuxury.com
blocks.idea: Sell top designer labels online, including LVMH's own.
blocks.decision: He believed luxury would move online, while skeptics doubted it. BoF says some now argue that LVMH was simply too early.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in 2000 by LVMH, selling names like Dior, Fendi and Marc Jacobs.
blocks.funding: LVMH's own money. The amount was not disclosed in the sources we read.
blocks.whatHappened: Top brands were hard to win, and BoF cites poor strategy and execution. Retail sales stopped on 26 July 2009. That made LVMH wary of digital for years, while rivals raced ahead. It came back in 2017 with a site called 24 Sèvres.
blocks.lesson: Being too early looks exactly like being wrong. If you try again, change the plan and not just the logo.

blocks.name: La Samaritaine
blocks.idea: A huge old department store beside the Seine in the heart of Paris, plus the land under it.
blocks.decision: Prime real estate that could become a landmark for tourists.
blocks.howStarted: LVMH bought 55% in January 2001. Then in 2005 the store had to close, because its old glass floors were not fire safe.
blocks.funding: €256 million for the first stake. LVMH took full ownership in 2010.
blocks.whatHappened: It stayed shut for 16 years. LVMH spent €750 million rebuilding it, with a hotel, restaurants and 96 social-housing flats. It reopened on 23 June 2021, during a pandemic, in a Paris with no tourists.
blocks.lesson: Some assets take a generation to pay. Only an owner who cannot be fired can wait 16 years.

blocks.name: Donna Karan and DKNY
blocks.idea: Buy a big American fashion name after Gucci's owner poached Alexander McQueen from LVMH.
blocks.decision: TIME reported the bid came days after that poaching. It looked like a very public answer to his rival.
blocks.howStarted: He bought the company that owned the name in January 2001, and then finished buying the listed company that November.
blocks.funding: LVMH's money: about $643 million in total.
blocks.whatHappened: It never became a star. In 2016 LVMH sold the loss-making business to G-III for $650 million. Fifteen years, and roughly the same price. Ten years later G-III also bought part of Marc Jacobs.
blocks.lesson: Do not buy things to win an argument. Fifteen years of holding produced almost nothing.

blocks.name: De Beers Diamond Jewellers
blocks.idea: A jewellery chain using the world's most famous diamond name, run with De Beers.
blocks.decision: In 2001 LVMH had no branded jewellery of its own, and this was a quick way in.
blocks.howStarted: Agreed in January 2001, cleared by the EU that July, with its base in London.
blocks.funding: A 50–50 joint venture. Amounts were not disclosed.
blocks.whatHappened: The chain reached 32 stores in 17 markets. In March 2017 De Beers bought LVMH out for an undisclosed sum. By then LVMH owned Bulgari and no longer needed it.
blocks.lesson: A joint venture is often a bridge. Fine, as long as you can see the far side.

blocks.name: Hermès stake
blocks.idea: Own a big piece of the one French luxury house he could never buy, a family-controlled maker of Birkin bags.
blocks.decision: LVMH always called it a financial investment. France's market regulator later doubted that, saying the method was built to avoid disclosure.
blocks.howStarted: It bought 4.9% in 2001–02, staying just under the 5% reporting line, then used equity swaps. Its boss got two hours' warning before the October 2010 announcement.
blocks.funding: LVMH cash and financial contracts with banks.
blocks.whatHappened: It reached 23.1%. Hermès's families locked up more than 50% in a new holding company, and LVMH paid an €8 million fine. In 2014 it gave its shares to its own shareholders and promised not to buy more for five years, with a €2.81 billion gain.
blocks.lesson: There are limits. A determined family with voting control can stop anyone, even the largest player in the field.

blocks.name: Les Echos, Le Parisien, Paris Match and the media group
blocks.idea: A leading French business daily, then a national daily, then a famous picture magazine.
blocks.decision: He had long wanted a place in French media. The Les Echos newsroom fought him for six months, fearing for its independence.
blocks.howStarted: LVMH already owned La Tribune, the rival business paper, and had to give it up to buy Les Echos, on orders from the competition authorities.
blocks.funding: LVMH's own money: €240 million for Les Echos from Pearson in 2007, a reported €50 million for Le Parisien in 2015, and an enterprise value of €120 million for Paris Match in 2024.
blocks.whatHappened: To sell La Tribune he had to add €34 million in capital and pay each of its 130 journalists €5,000. The group now also includes Radio Classique and Investir.
blocks.lesson: Owning the press gives you a voice, and it also makes every journalist in the country watch you more closely.

blocks.name: Carrefour
blocks.idea: A surprise: a luxury king buying into the world's second-biggest supermarket chain, with plans to unlock the value of its property.
blocks.decision: Colony Capital, a US property fund, talked him into it. He called it strategic and long term. It had nothing to do with luxury, and his family holding, not LVMH, took the risk.
blocks.howStarted: They set up a Luxembourg company called Blue Capital and bought 9.1% in March 2007.
blocks.funding: €3.23 billion, paying €50.94 a share. €2.4 billion of that was bank debt from Natixis and RBS. Debt makes a bet bigger, and it makes the losses bigger too.
blocks.whatHappened: The financial crisis came next. By October 2011 the share was €16.85, down 67%, and dividends did not cover the interest. Blue Capital was split up in 2013 and Colony left in 2017. In September 2021 Arnault sold his last 5.7% at €16 a share, for €724 million.
blocks.lesson: Great in one industry does not mean great in all of them. Borrowed money turns a wrong idea into a very expensive one.

blocks.text: Biggest personal flop: bought at about €51, sold at €16. Fourteen years later.
Scale, and the art of pruning

blocks.name: Bulgari
blocks.idea: A top Italian jeweller, which made LVMH a serious force in jewellery at last.
blocks.decision: The Hermès door was closing, and jewellery gave LVMH more reach in emerging markets. He paid a very high premium to get it.
blocks.howStarted: The family agreed privately and signed on 5 March 2011, then LVMH announced it two days later.
blocks.funding: €4.3 billion in total. €1.9 billion was in new LVMH shares, and the family received 16.5 million shares priced at €113. The rest was cash to minority shareholders. The premium was about 60%.
blocks.whatHappened: Paolo and Nicola Bulgari stayed on as chairman and vice-chairman, and their relative Francesco Trapani joined LVMH's top team to run all watches and jewellery. In 2026 LVMH said Bulgari's new high-jewellery line brought record revenue.
blocks.lesson: Pay a family in your own shares and they become your partners. It also keeps them interested for years.

blocks.name: Loro Piana
blocks.idea: An Italian maker of luxury cashmere and wool.
blocks.decision: It added a rare top-end Italian textile name. Reuters calls it the cashmere king.
blocks.howStarted: LVMH bought 80% in December 2013.
blocks.funding: €2 billion for the 80%. In January 2026 LVMH paid €1 billion more for a further 14%. By our arithmetic, the implied value of the whole firm nearly tripled, from about €2.5 billion to about €7.1 billion.
blocks.whatHappened: It became one of the group's star performers. But in July 2025 a Milan court put it under monitoring over labour abuse at subcontractors. The court lifted that early in April 2026, after the company cut ties with more than 100 suppliers.
blocks.lesson: When your brand promises perfection, you answer for every workshop in the chain, including those you never visit.

blocks.name: Young labels and side bets: Edun, Kirkwood, Fenty, Stella McCartney, Off-White, Patou
blocks.idea: Small stakes in young designers and celebrities, hoping to find the next big house. Rihanna's Fenty, Virgil Abloh's Off-White and Bono's Edun were the headline names.
blocks.decision: After Lacroix he rarely built from nothing, so this was the cheap way of trying: buy in early, and let the founder do the work.
blocks.howStarted: Each deal was with the founder: 49% of Edun in 2009, 52% of Nicholas Kirkwood in 2013, 50.01% of Fenty in 2019, 60% of Off-White in 2021.
blocks.funding: LVMH cash. Prices were mostly undisclosed.
blocks.whatHappened: Nearly all ended. Edun went back to its founders in 2018, Kirkwood in 2020. Fenty fashion was put on hold in February 2021. Off-White was sold in 2024, Stella McCartney's stake in January 2025, and Patou in July 2026.
blocks.lesson: Small bets are how a giant buys learning. Expect most of them to fail, and keep each one small enough not to matter.

blocks.name: Rimowa and Belmond
blocks.idea: A German luggage maker founded in 1898, then a group of luxury hotels, trains and river cruises that began with Venice's Hotel Cipriani.
blocks.decision: Both push the group further into travel, beyond shop products.
blocks.howStarted: Rimowa was agreed in October 2016, and Belmond was announced in late 2018.
blocks.funding: €640 million for 80% of Rimowa. $2.6 billion in equity for Belmond, $3.2 billion including its debt.
blocks.whatHappened: Both are still in the group. LVMH reported that Rimowa had good momentum in 2026. His son Alexandre helped run Rimowa, a training job for the next generation.
blocks.lesson: Use smaller companies to test your heirs before you hand them the big ones.

blocks.name: Tiffany & Co.
blocks.idea: America's most famous jeweller, the biggest luxury brand deal ever according to Forbes.
blocks.decision: He wanted more weight in jewellery, and a big American name.
blocks.howStarted: Agreed on 24 November 2019 at $135 a share, about $16.2 billion. Then the pandemic arrived, and he tried to get out of it.
blocks.funding: LVMH itself. No outside investors are named in the sources we read.
blocks.whatHappened: After lawsuits in Delaware, the price was cut to $131.50 a share, saving about $425 million. The deal closed in January 2021 at about $15.8 billion. Watches and jewellery revenue was up 8% organically in the first nine months of 2026, even as fashion fell.
blocks.lesson: Read the contract before a crisis. His case rested on the words that were not in it: no exception for pandemics.

blocks.name: L Capital, later L Catterton
blocks.idea: A private equity firm for consumer brands. Private equity means investing in companies that are not on the stock market, usually to sell them later at a profit.
blocks.decision: A fund could back consumer brands too small for LVMH itself, alongside outside investors.
blocks.howStarted: Founded in 2001 with LVMH and Groupe Arnault's support, it was led by Daniel Piette. Arnault's family had also invested in America's Catterton since 1998.
blocks.funding: LVMH, Groupe Arnault and outside investors. In 2016 the funds merged with Catterton: 60% owned by its partners, 40% by LVMH and Groupe Arnault.
blocks.whatHappened: At its creation it targeted more than $12 billion under management. Investments have included Sandro and Maje, Ba&sh and Gant.
blocks.lesson: Set up a way to learn from companies too small or too strange for your main business.

blocks.name: Aglaé Ventures and Agache
blocks.idea: The family's own venture arm, which puts money into technology companies far from luxury.
blocks.decision: CNBC notes that the family fortune is so concentrated in LVMH that it has little reason to invest in more luxury. Technology spreads the risk.
blocks.howStarted: Run from family holding Agache. Agache also bought the historic trunk maker Moynat in 2010, as a private side project.
blocks.funding: Family money. Amounts are usually not disclosed.
blocks.whatHappened: It has made 153 investments since 2017, CNBC reported in 2024, including AI firms such as H and Photoroom. The family was also an early backer of Netflix in 1999, Spotify in 2014 and Airbnb in 2015. Forbes adds TikTok's parent, ByteDance.
blocks.lesson: One rich person's Netflix stake and Boo.com stake came from the same year. Early investing is mostly misses, and one hit pays for them.

blocks.name: Fondation Louis Vuitton
blocks.idea: An art museum in the Bois de Boulogne in Paris, in a building by Frank Gehry.
blocks.decision: He presented it as a gift to France.
blocks.howStarted: The project was announced in 2006 at an estimated €100 million.
blocks.funding: LVMH companies, using a 2003 French law that lets firms deduct 60% of gifts from their tax bills.
blocks.whatHappened: The auditors at France's Cour des comptes put the final building cost near €790 million and the tax reduction at about €518 million. An anti-corruption group filed a complaint in 2018. LVMH said the same report raised no objection to its legality, and we found no report of any court ruling against it.
blocks.lesson: Giving is good marketing. When most of the bill goes through the tax system, expect the public to ask questions.

blocks.name: Paris FC
blocks.idea: A small second-division football club in a city ruled by Paris Saint-Germain. The plan is to build through local youth talent.
blocks.decision: Sport gives global attention. LVMH had just sponsored the Paris Olympics and signed a ten-year Formula 1 deal. His son Antoine fronts this one.
blocks.howStarted: Agache, the family holding, took 52.4% on 29 November 2024, with Red Bull taking 10.6%.
blocks.funding: Family money through Agache Sport. The price was not disclosed.
blocks.whatHappened: The club won promotion to France's top league on 2 May 2025, within six months, giving Paris two top-flight teams for the first time in 35 years. In October 2026 Le Parisien reported that Antoine Arnault would replace longtime president Pierre Ferracci, who is selling his remaining 29.8%.
blocks.lesson: Give your children real projects with public scoreboards. There is no hiding from a league table.

blocks.text: Add it up and the record is sobering. From this list, Lacroix, Boo.com, Zebank, eLuxury, Phillips, Donna Karan, Carrefour and most of the young labels lost money or went nowhere. __He is not a man who never misses. He is a man whose few big wins are so large that they swallow all the misses.__ In 2025, fashion and leather goods, led by Louis Vuitton and Dior, earned about three-quarters of the group's operating profit.
Very important: one giant win can pay for ten failures.

Some of his biggest targets never fell at all. Hermès held out. BusinessWeek reported in 1994, citing well-placed sources, that he was looking at L'Oréal, a company then bigger than LVMH, and no such deal ever happened. The Art Newspaper wrote that he had once thought about buying Sotheby's. Even for him, wanting something was not enough.

chapters.title: The Dead Dog and the Palace Coup

blocks.text: In 1984 Boussac was the kind of company nobody sane wanted. Its factories were so old that the EU's top court later noted some machinery dated from before the First World War. Its debts had reached ==3.68 billion francs== by 1981. France's government had poured in public money just to keep it alive. Almost the whole group had gone into court-supervised receivership in 1981.

There were still bidders, because of what sat inside. Arnault was then a small property developer of 35, known to the French press as Tintin. He had no experience in fashion or textiles. What he did have was a friend who showed him the file, family links to the Willot brothers who had owned Boussac, and a banker named Antoine Bernheim at Lazard. __Bernheim was the real turning point: a young man with little money had found someone who could assemble a lot of it.__
He was 35 and had never run a fashion business.
How do you buy a 400-million-franc company with 90 million?

This is the part founders should study closely. The whole purchase cost 400 million francs. Arnault's side put in just 90 million of that, and Les Echos reported that part of even that sum may have been borrowed from Crédit Lyonnais, then a state-owned bank. Lazard, Banque Worms, two oil-company subsidiaries and a little-known Lebanese fund provided the rest. Two years later he needed another 400 million francs to buy out the Willot brothers' last shares, so he sold part of his own holding company to more partners.

For example: think of a holding company as a company whose only job is to own other companies. If you own 51% of a holding company, and it owns 51% of the next one, you control that second company while owning only about 26% of it. Add more layers and the share you need keeps shrinking. A French banker worked out in 1985 that three layers could give control for capital worth about 13% of the assets at the bottom.

The government chose him in December 1984. A clip from the French archives shows why: of the two final bids, his looked like the cheapest socially. Staff would fall from 15,000 to 12,000 with no compulsory redundancies, and he gave himself two years to make the industrial business profitable. On 16 December he wrote to the prime minister asking for financial help. The answer came the next day.

Then came the part that made him famous and hated in equal measure. Within about two years Boussac was profitable. Press accounts say he got there by cutting about 9,000 jobs and selling the nappy business and much of the textile arm, for a windfall reported at between $400 million and $500 million. ABC News, among others, says the deal had been approved on his promise to keep the group and its workforce going, and that within five years he had sold nearly everything but Dior. __He picked up a nickname that stuck: the Terminator.__
Remember both things: brilliant deal, broken promise. Both are true.
The public money question

Forty years later, the money is still argued about. In December 2025 the French TV investigation Cash Investigation published a Finance Ministry note listing 633.1 million francs of state aid to Boussac, roughly €211 million in today's money. It set that against the 400 million francs paid for the company. LVMH replied that more than a billion francs had to be repaid to the state, and that it did repay them.

The EU's own record adds an important detail that the TV report did not stress. The Commission's 1987 decision says the aid was paid between June 1982 and January 1985, so __most of it reached Boussac before Arnault arrived__. It found the aid illegal, because France had not notified it, and ordered 338.56 million francs to be returned. France went to court, and in February 1990 the judges rejected its core arguments that the aid was acceptable. The TV report adds that LVMH was made to repay part of it in 1995.

There is one last irony. In May 2025 Arnault told a French Senate inquiry on public aid to big companies that it is very bad for the state to get involved in running private firms. The journalists at Cash Investigation asked whether he had forgotten how his own career began.
The fight inside LVMH

By 1988 he was ready for something far bigger. In June 1987 Moët Hennessy and Louis Vuitton had merged to create LVMH, then a group with projected 1988 revenues of $2.6 billion. The merger was a mistake in one important way. Its two leaders could not stand each other.

On one side was Alain Chevalier, 56, the head of Moët Hennessy. On the other side was Henry Racamier, 76, who had married into the Vuitton family and grown the luggage maker's sales from under $15 million in 1977 to over $380 million in 1987. Each kept his own staff, his own PR team and his own advisers. When heavy trading in May 1988 hinted at a possible takeover, Chevalier called his friend at Guinness and asked it to take a 20% stake as protection.

Racamier hated that idea, and he went looking for a friend of his own. He picked Arnault. It may be the worst business decision of his long life. __He had invited in the one person who wanted the whole house.__
Never ask a shark to settle a fight in your pool.

Arnault had gained control partly with warrants issued in the late 1980s, and Racamier's side asked the courts to cancel them. If that worked, Racamier was expected to try to throw him out. The appeals court refused. Reuters reported the confirmed stake as 34.5% of the votes, while the New York Times reported 43.5% of the shares.

blocks.text: The way he paid for it was just as bold as the fight. He needed ==7.3 billion francs==, more than eighteen times the price of Boussac, and raised it through a giant share sale at Dior plus a partner company with Guinness. Five holding-company layers then stood between his family and LVMH, each packed with friends and investors. Les Echos called it a finance pump. __In six years he had gone from a Florida housing project in trouble to running France's largest publicly owned company.__

He was not gentle after winning. He purged the top Vuitton executives, and the takeover gave him a reputation for ruthlessness that followed him for decades. Many admired his nerve all the same. One French financier at the time said people like him set a good example for the country's economy. Whether you see a hero or a villain usually depends on where you were standing in 1985.

Looking back, it seems that LVMH only ever goes up. That is an illusion created by distance. The group has been hit hard at least five times since 1990, and one of Arnault's personal investments lost billions on paper. He has also caused wounds of his own. None of these moments was a real bankruptcy scare at LVMH itself, and we found no proof of one. But in each, he was forced to change course.
1. The tower of debt, 1990–1993

The first shock arrived almost as soon as he won. The Gulf War and a recession hit the luxury market from 1991. Shares in Financière Agache, his top luxury holding, had halved during 1990. Champagne sales in Britain fell 40% in 1991 alone. By January 1993 LVMH was warning that profits would drop about 20%.

The real fear was the pyramid. Remember those holding-company layers? At the top sat Arnault & Associés, which his family controlled at 60%. The Independent wrote that this firm was worth under £300 million, yet it controlled an empire worth at least ten times more. Because many companies in the chain were private, __nobody outside could say how much debt the Arnault empire really carried.__
A pyramid is great going up. Terrifying when the top shakes.

He got out through selling and simplifying. In 1991 he sold control of Conforama to Pinault for over 3 billion francs in cash, and cleaned up his holdings. Then in January 1994 he unwound the Guinness cross-holding, which brought LVMH 11 billion francs. London's press thought he had given away too much: one columnist said investors were amazed. BusinessWeek saw him a month later, in his office above Dior's Paris store, cheerful about the $1.9 billion now coming his way.
2. The DFS gamble and Asia, 1997–1998

LVMH bet $2.47 billion on duty-free shops in January 1997, just before the Asian financial crisis. It had even sold shares in Guinness to pay. Bob Miller, the DFS co-founder who stayed on, later described watching the market fall fast, and called it his lowest point emotionally. By mid-1999 Reuters still described LVMH as bouncing back from the Asian slump.
3. The year profit nearly vanished, 2001

The third crisis was self-inflicted. After his two-year spree, LVMH carried about €7 billion of debt, and in 2000 servicing it held net profit growth to just 4%. Operating margins had slid from about 25% in 1995 to about 17% in 2000. A Lehman analyst complained publicly that LVMH was putting capital into low-return businesses. LVMH hit back with a letter and a full-page ad in the New York Times, saying the company was thriving.

Then the 2001 numbers landed. Net income dropped from ==€722 million to €10 million==, down 99%. That came with a global slowdown, the September 11 attacks, and heavy losses at new businesses such as Phillips and Sephora. LVMH issued its fourth profit warning. Net debt stood at 95% of equity.

blocks.text: His response is the lesson. He stopped buying, and started selling. Phillips went, Lacroix went, Hard Candy and Urban Decay went. By 2005 The Independent counted 25 brands sold in five years, leaving about 50. He cut Sephora's losses by closing Japan. __LVMH's own 2001 report now talked about cash, and about focusing on its luxury brands.__ And that terrible year was also the year it booked the €774 million Gucci gain.
He bought for a decade. Then he had to learn how to sell.
4. The Carrefour hole, 2007–2011

The fourth blow fell on his private holdings rather than LVMH. His supermarket bet was mostly bank debt: €2.4 billion out of €3.23 billion. By October 2011 the shares were 67% below his entry price, and L'Agefi reported that the holding company had lost about €2 billion in value since 2007. Dividends did not even cover its interest bill. He stayed in for ten more years, and when he finally left, the price was still only €16.
5. The pandemic, 2020

In spring 2020, stores and factories closed across most countries for months, and international travel stopped. LVMH's revenue fell 17% to €44.7 billion, and its operating profit fell 28%. He was also in the middle of the Tiffany dispute, which we cover in the next chapter. Yet the rebound was sharp: 2021 revenue reached €64.2 billion and profit more than doubled.
6. The slump of 2024–2026

The latest shock may be the most worrying, because it is not a sudden event. It is a slow shift. Revenue slid from €86.2 billion in 2023 to €80.8 billion in 2025. Profit from recurring operations fell from €22.8 billion to €17.8 billion. Fashion and leather goods, the engine of the group, saw its margin fall from 39.9% to 35%. The third quarter of 2026 saw that division fall 5% organically, hit by weaker demand in China.

In early 2026 LVMH's shares had their worst start to a year on record, according to a Bloomberg analysis reported by Forbes. Conflict in the Middle East cut shopping in hubs like Dubai, and a trademark fight with a Chinese tea chain caused a backlash. On 10 September 2026 Arnault fell out of the top ten on Bloomberg's rich list, reportedly for the first time since 2017. In response, LVMH is doing what it did in 2002: selling Marc Jacobs, most of DFS and other side businesses.

blocks.text: Wounds he caused himself

Not every wound came from outside. In 2013 LVMH hired Bernard Squarcini, France's former domestic intelligence chief, as a consultant. Investigators later looked at whether he had used his contacts on LVMH's behalf, including watching François Ruffin, a journalist making the mocking documentary Merci Patron about Arnault and a family who lost their jobs at a supplier. In December 2021 a Paris judge approved a €10 million settlement, closing the criminal probe into the company and sparing it a public trial.

In March 2025 a Paris court convicted Squarcini, who received a four-year sentence with two years suspended and was fined €200,000. His lawyer said he would appeal. The court found him complicit in illegal surveillance of Ruffin. An LVMH security director was among those acquitted. Press-freedom group RSF welcomed the verdict but criticised the settlement for keeping responsibility higher up the chain from being tested in court. The European Court of Human Rights rejected Ruffin's challenge to that settlement as inadmissible in 2023.
Paying to avoid a trial does not make the headline disappear.

Then came Italy. In June 2024 a Milan court put a Dior handbag unit under court administration after a probe alleged that it had subcontracted work to Chinese-owned firms that mistreated workers. In July 2025 the same happened to Loro Piana, where police said some workers put in up to 90 hours a week. Loro Piana said it had not known about the subcontracting. In both cases the courts ended the measures early, in February 2025 and April 2026, after the companies changed suppliers and controls.

__There is a hard lesson in those cases for anyone who builds a brand: the higher your price, the further a scandal travels.__ A bag can cost thousands of euros, and a story about who stitched it can undo years of careful advertising. You can outsource the work. You cannot outsource the blame.

chapters.title: Four Fights That Made the Legend

blocks.text: Most founders fight competitors with products. Arnault often fought them with shares, lawyers and timing. Four battles show how he thinks better than any interview he has given. In one he won by making himself impossible to ignore. In one he lost the prize and pocketed a fortune. In one he was stopped. In the last he used a crisis to cut the price.
Round one: the £500 million nuisance

By May 1997 Guinness and Grand Metropolitan were planning a giant drinks merger, the company later called Diageo. Arnault had a problem: his stake in the merged firm would shrink below 7%, and he would lose his seat on the board. So he went on the attack. He said the merger triggered a clause in his 1994 agreement with Guinness, and announced he would buy back Guinness's 34% of Moët Hennessy.

Then he made an unusual move. He sold part of his Guinness shares and used the money to buy ==11% of GrandMet==, spending over £1 billion and becoming the largest shareholder in both companies. He flew around lobbying big investors with a rival plan to merge all three companies' drinks and split off Burger King and Pillsbury. He began arbitration that some estimates said could cost the merger up to £1 billion.

On a Saturday evening in October 1997, after months of secret talks, both sides settled. LVMH received £250 million in cash, plus £250 million more through a special dividend. It also got a board seat, an 11% stake in the new group and most of its drinks distribution network. __He gave up his plan to break up the company, but only after turning his objection into roughly £500 million.__ Bloomberg reported that he described the cash as the price of burying the hatchet.
Noticed? He did not need to win. He only needed to be expensive.

For example: if your opponent needs your vote to finish a deal, your vote has a price. Under the rules Arnault threatened to use, a shareholder meeting could have forced the merger to win a 75% vote. An 11% holder is suddenly very important when the required majority is that high.
Round two: the handbag war

In January 1999, Arnault was again buying quietly, this time Gucci. He insisted that his 5% stake was passive. By 26 January he held 34.4%. Gucci's boss, Domenico De Sole, sent a deal limiting his buying, and asked for a signature by a deadline on 17 February. At 5:01 pm that day the fax came back, on time, and with no signature.

De Sole's reply was one of the wildest moves in fashion history. Within a day he set up an employee share plan that created new shares equal to a 42% stake. It was a poison pill, a defence that makes a takeover much harder by flooding the market with new shares. Arnault's stake fell to about 20% in minutes. Then, in March 1999, Gucci sold that 42% to François Pinault's PPR for $3 billion, shortly before a scheduled meeting between the two sides. LVMH reportedly learned it from the news. PPR played the white knight, the friendly buyer who rescues a target from a hostile one.

Remember who Pinault was. In 1991 he had bought Conforama from Arnault in a friendly deal. Arnault later admitted in his book that he should have been more on his guard. LVMH offered $81 and then $85 a share, sued in the Netherlands, and tried to freeze the deal. In May 1999 a Dutch court upheld the sale to PPR. A further court inquiry cleared the share plan. The lawsuits and insults ran for two and a half years.
It is always flattering to be imitated.

blocks.text: The ending surprised people who think in winners and losers. Under a settlement dated 10 September 2001, PPR bought 8.6 million of LVMH's Gucci shares at $94 each, $806 million. In December LVMH sold its last 11.6 million shares to Crédit Lyonnais for $1.04 billion. De Sole called the exit good riddance, while LVMH's spokesman called it a legal and financial success. Its annual report shows a ==€774 million gain==. __Pinault got Gucci. Arnault got the cash, in the same year his own profit almost disappeared.__

blocks.text: Round three: the family that said no

Hermès was different, because it was owned by a family who would not sell. LVMH bought 4.9% in 2001–02, carefully staying below the 5% mark at which French law requires a public statement. Then it used equity swaps. An equity swap is a contract with a bank that pays you as if you held a share, without you actually owning it. Those contracts did not need to be declared under the rules at that time.

In October 2010 LVMH asked its banks to settle the swaps in actual shares, and suddenly announced 14.2%. Hermès chief executive Patrick Thomas got the news only two hours before the market did, in a phone call from Arnault while cycling in the French Alps. LVMH said it had no plan to take control and described the stake as friendly. Hermès's chairman told Le Figaro that the company had never seen attacks like these in 174 years.

__This time he met an opponent he could not buy, scare or wait out.__ Within weeks, the founding families pooled more than 50% of the shares in a private holding company with first refusal on any family sale. The market regulator agreed, and that ended any real takeover path. Arnault reached 23.1% and could go no further. Lawsuits flew both ways, including a Hermès criminal complaint that LVMH called unfounded.

In July 2013 the AMF, France's market regulator, fined LVMH a record €8 million. It said LVMH's method had been unusual and had avoided disclosure, though its main formal criticism concerned the timing of the disclosure. The AMF had sought €10 million. LVMH first said it would appeal, then dropped that plan. Arnault told shareholders that the company had ended up owning the shares unexpectedly. The regulator's investigators saw it differently.

The end came through a court-brokered peace in September 2014. LVMH gave its 23.2% stake to its own shareholders: two Hermès shares for every 41 LVMH shares. All sides dropped their lawsuits and agreed to a five-year freeze on further buying. LVMH booked a ==€2.81 billion gain==. The Arnault family's own company was left with about 8.5% of Hermès, a stake it partly used three years later to help pay for Dior. Forbes still lists him as a minority holder today.
Lesson: voting control beats money. Every founder should understand this.
Round four: the deal he tried to escape

On 24 November 2019, LVMH agreed to buy Tiffany at $135 a share. Soon after, Covid shut down shops around the world. The virus dealt a big blow to luxury, and people wondered if $16 billion was now too much. Then, on 31 August 2020, something strange arrived: a letter from France's foreign minister saying that Arnault should delay the closing until 6 January 2021, because of a trade row with the US.

The letter would have pushed the closing past the deal's November deadline. On 9 September LVMH's board announced that it could not complete the purchase. Tiffany sued that same day in Delaware, the US state where it is registered. It accused LVMH of using excuses to force a lower price, and it pointed to press reports claiming that LVMH had procured the letter itself. LVMH rejected those claims and sued back on 28 September.

LVMH's main legal argument is worth knowing. A material adverse effect, or MAE, is a clause that lets a buyer walk away if the target's business suffers serious damage before closing. LVMH argued that hundreds of other merger agreements listed pandemics as an exception, while this one did not. It had exceptions for cyberattacks, Hong Kong protests and France's Yellow Vest movement, but not for pandemics. Nobody knows whether a judge would have agreed, because the case never reached the 5 January trial date that had been set.

Late in October 2020 the two sides settled at ==$131.50 a share==. That shaved about $425 million off a $16 billion deal. Some analysts wondered why LVMH had started such a bitter fight for such a small cut. Ending it did save potentially costly legal fees. Tiffany shareholders approved it on 30 December, and it closed in January 2021. He paid close to the original price. In the first nine months of 2026, the division Tiffany belongs to was among the group's strongest.

blocks.text: Put the four fights side by side and you can see a method. He buys in early, while others are still deciding. He moves faster than the rules expect. He uses the courts as a tool for buying time. __And he nearly always has an exit that pays, even when the main prize is lost.__ You can admire that as a skill, and you can also see why so many people in French business have feared and disliked him for it.

Arnault's fortune is not a pile of cash. It is almost entirely one thing: his family's stake in LVMH. Forbes put his wealth at ==$117.4 billion on 1 November 2026==, ranking him 17th in the world. That is about half of his Forbes peak of $233 billion. To understand how it was built, follow one number across forty years.

blocks.text: From 90 million francs to one of the world's great stakes

Start with that 90 million francs in 1984. Twelve years later, in June 1996, Les Echos worked out that he owned 19% of LVMH, a company worth 110 billion francs. By our arithmetic, that stake was worth about ==21 billion francs==. That is roughly 230 times the original cheque, helped along by partners and debt that the headline number does not show. Les Echos called it a feat that would be hard to match in French capitalism.

For example: if your family owned one floor of a building, you would not control much. Arnault owned a thin slice at the top of a tall tower. Every rise in LVMH's value flowed up the tower to that thin slice, while the debts along the way stayed fixed. That is called leverage, and it is why his fortune rose so fast on the way up. It also explains the panic in 1993.

Over the next decades he kept thickening that slice. Forbes first listed him in 1997 at $3.6 billion. By 2002 he and his family held 48% of LVMH, though his wealth had fallen to $7 billion from $12.8 billion two years earlier. By the April 2022 shareholders' meeting the family held 47.83% of the capital and 63.89% of votes. By December 2025 it was 49.8%. In September 2026 it stood at 50.33%, helped by the family's own purchases. LVMH also bought back €2.3 billion of its own shares in the first nine months of 2026, which tends to lift every remaining holder's share.

__This is the quiet secret of his wealth: he has spent forty years buying more of the same company.__ The 2025 Christian Dior annual report says Agache has kept up steady buying since 1987, and that its stake recently went past 50%. Billionaires.Africa put his 2025 purchases at about €1.4 billion, at an average price of about €566. The stock later fell far below that.
Most founders sell over time. He keeps buying. Think about that.
The number behind the number

LVMH's market value decides nearly everything. On 12 October 2026 the shares closed at €384.50, down about 41% in 2026, and more than half below their 2023 record. With about 498 million shares in issue at the end of 2025, the company was worth about €191 billion. By our arithmetic the family's 50.33% was worth about €96 billion that day. The gap to Forbes's figure probably reflects later share moves and his other assets, though Forbes does not publish its full sums.

In April 2023 those same shares passed €900, and LVMH became the first European company worth $500 billion. In December 2022 Bloomberg had made Arnault the world's richest person, and he remained at or near the top on and off until 2024. Think about that for a moment. On Forbes's numbers, the paper fall from his peak is about $116 billion, which is more than the entire fortune of almost everyone else on its list.
The cash machine

Where does the value come from? In 2025 fashion and leather goods, led by Louis Vuitton and Dior, earned €13.2 billion of the group's €17.8 billion operating profit, or about 74%. Its operating margin was 35%, even after a poor year. Selective retailing, led by Sephora, made €1.78 billion. Watches and jewellery made €1.51 billion. Wines and spirits made €1.02 billion, and perfumes and cosmetics made €727 million.

That profit turns into real money for the family through dividends, which are a share of profit paid out to shareholders in cash. LVMH paid ==€13 a share== for 2025. By our arithmetic, on 50.33% of about 498 million shares, that comes to roughly €3.3 billion a year. So even with the shares falling, the family's holdings collect more each year than almost any start-up ever raises. Income like that can fund football clubs, venture bets and more LVMH shares without selling anything.

blocks.text: Taming the tower

The pyramid that scared investors in 1993 has been shrinking for thirty years. From five layers in the late 1980s, it was down to three by 1996. In April 2017 came the big step. The family offered about €12 billion for the 25.9% of Christian Dior it did not own, paying partly with Hermès shares. At the same time, the Dior holding sold Christian Dior Couture to LVMH for €6.5 billion, which is 15.6 times its annual cash earnings. Investors had asked for a simpler structure for years.

Then, on 23 September 2026, came the plan that may be his last great piece of financial engineering. Financière Agache would merge into Agache, Agache would merge into Christian Dior, and the result would be renamed Agache. The family would offer cash for the 2.44% of Dior it does not hold, about €1.63 billion, with an illustrative price of €469.05 a share. The vote is expected in December 2026, and the tender offer in early 2027. This was still a plan, subject to regulators and shareholders, when this book was written.

The legal form matters most. The new company would be a limited joint-stock partnership, a French structure which the family itself says is meant to ensure its control continues. Arnault would be the managing partner, a job that is much harder for ordinary shareholders to challenge. The family adopted this same form in 2022 for Agache, with a plan under which, later, a company owned equally by his five children would take over the role. __At 77, he is building a machine designed to keep control in the family, whichever child ends up in charge.__

He has also moved the rules that might have pushed him out. In 2022 shareholders raised the age limit for LVMH's chief executive from 75 to 80. All five children work in the group, and his son Antoine now also fronts the football club. For a family that began with a builder in Roubaix in 1922, that is four generations of the same instinct: keep hold of the company.

blocks.text: Here is what to take from this chapter. __A fortune like this does not come from a brilliant exit. It comes from never exiting the one thing that compounds.__ He sold nappies, furniture, textiles, a bank, an auction house, and dozens of brands. He never sold his grip on the company at the centre. Yet that also means his wealth now rises and falls almost entirely with one stock, one industry and the mood of shoppers in China. In luxury, as in life, the concentration that makes you is also the thing that can hurt you the most.

factCheck.method: Primary documents came first: LVMH press releases, annual reports and investor pages, Christian Dior SE filings, SEC exhibits from Tiffany and Diageo, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange notice on DFS, the European Commission's 1987 Boussac decision and the 1990 Court of Justice case file. Then contemporaneous press from Les Echos, Le Monde, Reuters, the New York Times, Bloomberg/BusinessWeek, WSJ, The Economist, Forbes, WWD, TIME, the Guardian and the Independent. Several NYT archive pages could be read only in part, so those claims rest on the visible text and on other outlets. Amounts marked 'our arithmetic' are calculations: FF 110bn x 19% (1996 stake), €384.50 x 497.7m shares x 50.33% (family stake at 12 Oct 2026), €13 x 497.7m x 50.33% (dividend), and €2bn/80% vs €1bn/14% (Loro Piana). Net worth is the Forbes real-time profile as of 1 Nov 2026. Reddit, forums and low-quality biography sites were used as leads only and are not cited. In line with this project's copyright limit, only one short direct quote is used; everything else is paraphrased. To verify at the merge stage: the operative part of the Court of Justice's 1990 judgment (we read paragraphs rejecting France's arguments, not the final ruling text) and the later rise in LVMH's CEO age limit above 80, which we could not source and left out.
